\paragraph{Methodological constraints.}
Our internal-reasoning baseline uses single-pass ReAct~\citep{react-2023}. Reflexion~\citep{reflexion-2023} reduces death rate from 42.9\% to 31.4\% (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}), but more aggressive self-correction or Tree-of-Thought backtracking~\citep{tot-2023} may further reduce internal death rates. Episode-level labels assign a single routing preference to entire episodes, which may be suboptimal for individual steps (particularly those preceding death events). However, only 0.3\% of training steps exhibit directional conflict with episode labels (7/2,040); the dominant issue is not mislabeling but the 97.4\% step-level tie rate, which leaves the router with almost no per-step signal to learn from. Training on pure-strategy trajectories also introduces distribution shift at deployment~\citep{dagger-2011}. More broadly, projecting episode-level labels onto 10--50 sequential steps with path-dependent state introduces compounding error: early routing decisions alter the state trajectory, potentially invalidating later labels derived from the episode outcome.

\section{Conclusion}

We presented a diagnostic framework for decomposing routing signal in modular LLM agents via episode-level counterfactual analysis. Applied to ScienceWorld (245 episodes, 11 task types), 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry; four intervention axes confirm this is robust. Cross-domain probes support framework predictions: MATH confirms the null without catastrophic failure; ALFWorld identifies information asymmetry. Future work should target environments with intermediate death regimes (NetHack~\citep{nethack-2020} combat, Crafter~\citep{crafter-2022} with tuned difficulty) and stronger backbones.

\paragraph{Practitioner implications.}
We formalize a three-stage diagnostic (${\sim}$50-episode pilot $\to$ death-rate differential $\to$ death-label fraction) with thresholds in Appendix~\ref{app:decision-framework}; retrospective validation confirms correct predictions for all four conditions (Qwen-7B, Llama-8B, Qwen-72B, MATH). Our router training consumed ${\sim}$200 GPU-hours without exceeding always-deterministic; this framework could have predicted that from a 50-episode pilot. A separate deployment concern: counterfactual labels derive from pure-strategy episodes, but a deployed router produces mixed trajectories with different state distributions~\citep{dagger-2011}; the 4B router's end-to-end score ($-12.03$, below always-deterministic $-9.47$) may partly reflect this shift.

lines: All 105 internal-strategy deaths trace to misuse of \texttt{focus on [object]}, the answer-submission action, as a general interaction command (Appendix~\ref{app:failure-modes}). The root cause is grounding failure: agents parse task descriptions correctly but cannot map understanding to valid primitives; the majority of death episodes show effective reasoning in non-fatal steps before a single grounding error triggers irreversible failure. The internal strategy's higher death count (105 vs.\ 40) reflects more frequent entry into catastrophic states, not different within-episode behavior (${\sim}5\%$ \texttt{focus on} rate in both). \texttt{find-non-living-thing} (zero deaths) uses \texttt{focus on} more frequently than death-prone tasks---non-living objects are the majority class, so indiscriminate submissions rarely trigger death; lethality is a joint function of action misuse and answer distribution. Direct grounding interventions reduce but do not eliminate vulnerability ($48.0\% \to 29.0\%$ via action-space filter; Appendix~\ref{app:grounding-ablation}).
\paragraph{Practitioner implications.}

-We formalize a three-stage diagnostic (${\sim}$50-episode pilot $\to$ death-rate differential $\to$ death-label fraction) with thresholds in Appendix~\ref{app:decision-framework}; retrospective validation confirms correct predictions for all four conditions (Qwen-7B, Llama-8B, Qwen-72B, MATH). Our router training consumed ${\sim}$200 GPU-hours without exceeding always-deterministic; this framework could have predicted that from a 50-episode pilot. A separate deployment concern: counterfactual labels derive from pure-strategy episodes, but a deployed router produces mixed trajectories with different state distributions~\citep{dagger-2011}; the 4B router's end-to-end score ($-12.03$, below always-deterministic $-9.47$) may partly reflect this shift.

+A three-stage diagnostic (${\sim}$50-episode pilot $\to$ death-rate differential $\to$ death-label fraction; Appendix~\ref{app:decision-framework}) correctly predicts outcomes for all four conditions (Qwen-7B, Llama-8B, Qwen-72B, MATH). Our router training consumed ${\sim}$200 GPU-hours without exceeding always-deterministic; this diagnostic could have predicted that from a 50-episode pilot. Counterfactual labels also derive from pure-strategy episodes; the 4B router's end-to-end score ($-12.03$, below always-deterministic $-9.47$) may partly reflect distribution shift at deployment~\citep{dagger-2011}.
\paragraph{Framework applicability.}

The penalty-independent label fraction (78.9\%) is the primary diagnostic; DAF increases monotonically with $P$ (Appendix~\ref{app:penalty}). Preliminary pilots on MiniHack~\citep{minihack-2021} (0\% death, no monster spawning) and Crafter~\citep{crafter-2022} (100\% death, both strategies) produced no death asymmetry, illustrating two boundary conditions: environments lacking a death mechanism yield no routing signal (consistent with MATH), while environments where no strategy avoids death lack exploitable asymmetry. The framework requires an intermediate regime where strategy choice affects survival; NetHack~\citep{nethack-2020} combat tasks remain the most direct replication target \citep{balrog-2025,netplay-2024}.

   - Penalty-independent label fraction: 78.9% (75/95 non-tie labels)
   - Step-level directional conflict: 0.3% (7/2,040) — NOT 27.7%
   - Step-level tie rate: 97.4% (5,726/5,878 steps)
   - MDE for Reflexion: ~14pp at N=200, α=0.05, 80% power (NOT ~7pp)
   - Reflexion N=1→3: Δ=-13.5pp, z=2.75, p=0.003

     ```latex
     \paragraph{Scope of episode-level analysis.}
     At step level, 97.4\% of oracle comparisons yield ties (\S\ref{sec:collection}) and only 0.3\% of training steps exhibit directional conflict with episode labels. This near-complete absence of step-level signal---rather than label noise---explains why episode-level analysis is the appropriate granularity and why step-level router training approaches chance performance (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).
     ```

     \paragraph{Why the router fails: task-type-level signal.}
     The router diagnostic (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}) reveals a structural mismatch: death avoidance is a task-type-level binary property (10/11 types carry death risk), but step-level features correlate weakly because death risk depends on multi-step trajectories, not individual action semantics. The 4B router improves at episode level ($59.0\%$) without step-level gains ($56$--$59\%$), confirming task-type classification rather than generalizable features; cross-task-type transfer yields chance accuracy (49.2\%; Appendix~\ref{app:ablations}).
     
     \paragraph{Non-triviality of death dominance.}
     While death dominance follows from the penalty structure (\S\ref{sec:daf}), three properties were not predictable a priori: (i)~\emph{routing prior}---the oracle matches always-deterministic on 96.3\% of decisions (2.89-point improvement), and threshold routing with perfect death risk knowledge still cannot outperform always-deterministic (Appendix~\ref{sec:threshold-routing}), so the rational prior is ``do not route''; (ii)~\emph{intervention resistance}---retry ($43.5\%$), Reflexion ($34.0\%$), $10{\times}$ scaling ($30.6\%$), and action-space filtering ($29.0\%$) all leave ${\geq}$12~pp residual gaps to deterministic safety ($16.3\%$), with Reflexion and scaling converging to overlapping Wilson CIs suggesting a shared bound from lacking ground-truth state access; (iii)~\emph{cross-model stability}---Qwen-7B and Llama-8B show nearly identical internal vulnerability (${\sim}$42\%), and 72B scaling leaves death dominance intact (DAF $= 92.4\%$). More aggressive interventions (Tree-of-Thought~\citep{tot-2023}, process reward models) remain untested; we characterize a ceiling for the tested classes, not a universal bound.

Cross-domain probes validate predictions: no signal in MATH, information asymmetry in ALFWorld. Future work should target intermediate death regimes (NetHack~\citep{nethack-2020}, Crafter~\citep{crafter-2022}) and stronger backbones.

\section{Conclusion}

We presented a diagnostic framework for decomposing routing signal in modular LLM agents. Applied to ScienceWorld, 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry; four intervention axes confirm robustness. Cross-domain probes validate predictions: no signal in MATH, information asymmetry in ALFWorld. Future work should target intermediate death regimes (NetHack~\citep{nethack-2020}, Crafter~\citep{crafter-2022}) and stronger backbones.

lines: While death dominance follows from the penalty structure (\S\ref{sec:daf}), three properties were not predictable a priori: (i)~\emph{routing prior}---the oracle matches always-deterministic on 96.3\% of decisions (2.89-point improvement), and threshold routing with perfect death risk knowledge still cannot outperform always-deterministic (Appendix~\ref{sec:threshold-routing}), so the rational prior is ``do not route''; (ii)~\emph{intervention resistance}---retry ($43.5\%$), Reflexion ($34.0\%$), $10{\times}$ scaling ($30.6\%$), and action-space filtering ($29.0\%$) all leave ${\geq}$12~pp residual gaps to deterministic safety ($16.3\%$), with Reflexion and scaling converging to overlapping Wilson CIs suggesting a shared bound from lacking ground-truth state access; (iii)~\emph{cross-model stability}---Qwen-7B and Llama-8B show nearly identical internal vulnerability (${\sim}$42\%), and 72B scaling leaves death dominance intact (DAF $= 92.4\%$). More aggressive interventions (Tree-of-Thought~\citep{tot-2023}, process reward models) remain untested; we characterize a ceiling for the tested classes, not a universal bound.
\paragraph{Anatomy of catastrophic failure.}

-All 105 internal-strategy deaths trace to misuse of \texttt{focus on [object]}, the answer-submission action, as a general interaction command (Appendix~\ref{app:failure-modes}). The root cause is grounding failure: agents parse task descriptions correctly but cannot map understanding to valid primitives; the majority of death episodes show effective reasoning in non-fatal steps before a single grounding error triggers irreversible failure. The internal strategy's higher death count (105 vs.\ 40) reflects more frequent entry into catastrophic states, not different within-episode behavior (${\sim}5\%$ \texttt{focus on} rate in both). \texttt{find-non-living-thing} (zero deaths) uses \texttt{focus on} more frequently than death-prone tasks---non-living objects are the majority class, so indiscriminate submissions rarely trigger death; lethality is a joint function of action misuse and answer distribution. Direct grounding interventions reduce but do not eliminate vulnerability ($48.0\% \to 29.0\%$ via action-space filter; Appendix~\ref{app:grounding-ablation}).

\paragraph{Practitioner implications.}

A three-stage diagnostic (${\sim}$50-episode pilot $\to$ death-rate differential $\to$ death-label fraction; Appendix~\ref{app:decision-framework}) correctly predicts outcomes for all four conditions (Qwen-7B, Llama-8B, Qwen-72B, MATH). Our router training consumed ${\sim}$200 GPU-hours without exceeding always-deterministic; this diagnostic could have predicted that from a 50-episode pilot. Counterfactual labels also derive from pure-strategy episodes; the 4B router's end-to-end score ($-12.03$, below always-deterministic $-9.47$) may partly reflect distribution shift at deployment~\citep{dagger-2011}.

\section{Conclusion}

We presented a diagnostic framework for decomposing routing signal in modular LLM agents. Applied to ScienceWorld, 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry; four intervention axes confirm robustness. Cross-domain probes validate predictions: no signal in MATH, information asymmetry in ALFWorld. Future work should target intermediate death regimes (NetHack~\citep{nethack-2020}, Crafter~\citep{crafter-2022}) and stronger backbones.

- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.

- review: Review a pull request

content.content:
1	\section{Related Work}
2	
3	\paragraph{Tool Use and External Computation in LLMs.}
4	A growing body of work augments language models with external tools \citep{tool-learning-survey-2024}, spanning several functional categories.
5	\emph{Self-supervised} approaches learn tool invocation from loss signals: Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} inserts API calls filtered by perplexity reduction; ToolACE \cite{toolace-2025} curates synthetic data for function-calling accuracy.
6	\emph{Token-level} methods embed tools into the model vocabulary: ToolkenGPT \cite{toolkengpt-2023} represents tools as special tokens resolved at inference.
7	\emph{Task-level} decomposition routes subtasks to specialized modules: ART \cite{art-2023} generates tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} composes heterogeneous modules per subtask.
8	\emph{RL-based} methods learn routing policies from reward: ReTool \cite{retool-2025} discovers when code execution is preferable to chain-of-thought.
9	All focus on \emph{learning to use tools}; we ask a prior question: \emph{what signal drives the routing decision?}
10	Recent concurrent work sharpens this question: \citet{tool-overuse-illusion-2026} identify a cognitive-illusion effect where LLMs default to external tools even when internal knowledge suffices, finding that tool overuse correlates with model uncertainty rather than task difficulty. \citet{when2tool-2026} show tool-call decisions are encoded in hidden states before reasoning, \citet{tool-use-tax-2026} quantify a ``tool-use tax,'' and \citet{to-call-or-not-2026} propose a necessity, utility, and affordability framework. Our decomposition provides environment-grounded evidence: in ScienceWorld, 78.9\% of routing labels trace to catastrophic-failure prevention.
11	
12	\paragraph{Adaptive Computation and Routing.}
13	CogRouter \cite{cogrouter-2026} adapts reasoning depth per step, ARES \cite{ares-2026} selects among reasoning effort levels, Mixture-of-Recursions \cite{mixture-of-recursions-2025} learns token-level recursion depths, and MTRouter \cite{mtrouter-2026} addresses multi-turn routing.
14	RouteLLM \citep{routellm-2024} learns routers from preference data to select between strong and weak models.
15	These optimize \emph{how} to route; we reveal \emph{why} routing helps: in interactive environments, the dominant signal is catastrophic-failure avoidance.
16	
17	\paragraph{Counterfactual Evaluation in RL.}
18	Prior work generates counterfactual explanations for RL agents by perturbing individual actions within a fixed policy \citep{olson2021counterfactual, gajcin2023counterfactual, amitai2024explaining}.
19	Our approach differs in both purpose and granularity: we execute two complete episodes under different routing strategies, producing prospective paired comparisons that isolate routing signal \emph{before} any router is trained.
20	
21	\paragraph{LLM Agent Environments and Reasoning.}
22	ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022} serves as our primary testbed; Inner Monologue \cite{huang2022inner} grounds LLM planning in embodied feedback; Voyager \cite{wang2023voyager} demonstrates open-ended LLM agents; ALFWorld \cite{alfworld-2021} provides a complementary household environment; AgentBench \cite{agentbench-2024} offers systematic evaluation. \citet{zhou2024webarena} document common failure modes (premature termination, hallucinated actions) in web-based agents, consistent with our finding that state hallucination is the primary internal-strategy failure mechanism. ReAct \cite{react-2023} serves as our internal baseline; Reflexion \cite{reflexion-2023} extends this with verbal self-reflection; LATS \cite{lats-2024} adds tree search. SelfCheckGPT \cite{selfcheckgpt-2023} detects unreliable LLM outputs; our work shows that in interactive environments, such unreliability manifests as catastrophic death.
23	
24	\paragraph{Safe RL.}
25	Safe RL methods \citep{garcia2015comprehensive,tamar2015cvar,achiam2017cpo,crpo-2021,moldovan2012safe} enforce constraints in MDPs via risk-sensitive objectives, constrained optimization, or safe exploration; SafeRoute \citep{saferoute-2025} applies adaptive model selection for safety guardrails. These assume the agent can learn to avoid catastrophic states; our results show that computation mode routing already functions as an implicit safety mechanism---the deterministic strategy sidesteps catastrophic states entirely.
26

lines: Recent concurrent work sharpens this question: \citet{tool-overuse-illusion-2026} identify a cognitive-illusion effect where LLMs default to external tools even when internal knowledge suffices, finding that tool overuse correlates with model uncertainty rather than task difficulty. \citet{when2tool-2026} show tool-call decisions are encoded in hidden states before reasoning, \citet{tool-use-tax-2026} quantify a ``tool-use tax,'' and \citet{to-call-or-not-2026} propose a necessity, utility, and affordability framework. Our decomposition provides environment-grounded evidence: in ScienceWorld, 78.9\% of routing labels trace to catastrophic-failure prevention.
\paragraph{Adaptive Computation and Routing.}

-CogRouter \cite{cogrouter-2026} adapts reasoning depth per step, ARES \cite{ares-2026} selects among reasoning effort levels, Mixture-of-Recursions \cite{mixture-of-recursions-2025} learns token-level recursion depths, and MTRouter \cite{mtrouter-2026} addresses multi-turn routing.

+Adaptive routing traces back to learned halting policies \citep{graves2016act}. In the LLM era, CogRouter \cite{cogrouter-2026} adapts reasoning depth per step, ARES \cite{ares-2026} selects among reasoning effort levels, Mixture-of-Recursions \cite{mixture-of-recursions-2025} learns token-level recursion depths, and MTRouter \cite{mtrouter-2026} addresses multi-turn routing.
RouteLLM \citep{routellm-2024} learns routers from preference data to select between strong and weak models.
These optimize \emph{how} to route; we reveal \emph{why} routing helps: in interactive environments, the dominant signal is catastrophic-failure avoidance.

lines: ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022} serves as our primary testbed; Inner Monologue \cite{huang2022inner} grounds LLM planning in embodied feedback; Voyager \cite{wang2023voyager} demonstrates open-ended LLM agents; ALFWorld \cite{alfworld-2021} provides a complementary household environment; AgentBench \cite{agentbench-2024} offers systematic evaluation. \citet{zhou2024webarena} document common failure modes (premature termination, hallucinated actions) in web-based agents, consistent with our finding that state hallucination is the primary internal-strategy failure mechanism. ReAct \cite{react-2023} serves as our internal baseline; Reflexion \cite{reflexion-2023} extends this with verbal self-reflection; LATS \cite{lats-2024} adds tree search. SelfCheckGPT \cite{selfcheckgpt-2023} detects unreliable LLM outputs; our work shows that in interactive environments, such unreliability manifests as catastrophic death.
\paragraph{Safe RL.}

-Safe RL methods \citep{garcia2015comprehensive,tamar2015cvar,achiam2017cpo,crpo-2021,moldovan2012safe} enforce constraints in MDPs via risk-sensitive objectives, constrained optimization, or safe exploration; SafeRoute \citep{saferoute-2025} applies adaptive model selection for safety guardrails. lines: All 105 internal-strategy deaths trace to misuse of \texttt{focus on [object]}, the answer-submission action, as a general interaction command (Appendix~\ref{app:failure-modes}). The root cause is grounding failure: agents parse task descriptions correctly but cannot map understanding to valid primitives; the majority of death episodes show effective reasoning in non-fatal steps before a single grounding error triggers irreversible failure. The internal strategy's higher death count (105 vs.\ 40) reflects more frequent entry into catastrophic states, not different within-episode behavior (${\sim}5\%$ \texttt{focus on} rate in both); lethality depends jointly on misuse rate and answer distribution (\texttt{find-non-living-thing} has zero deaths despite high submission rate because non-living objects are the majority class). Direct grounding interventions reduce but do not eliminate vulnerability ($48.0\% \to 29.0\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:grounding-ablation}).
\paragraph{Practitioner implications.}

-A three-stage diagnostic (${\sim}$50-episode pilot $\to$ death-rate differential $\to$ death-label fraction; Appendix~\ref{app:decision-framework}) correctly predicts outcomes for all four conditions (Qwen-7B, Llama-8B, Qwen-72B, MATH). Counterfactual labels also derive from pure-strategy episodes; the 4B router's end-to-end score ($-12.03$, below always-deterministic $-9.47$) may partly reflect distribution shift at deployment~\citep{dagger-2011}.

The 4B router's end-to-end score ($-12.03$, below always-deterministic $-9.47$) may partly reflect distribution shift at deployment~\citep{dagger-2011}.
\paragraph{Framework applicability.}

The penalty-independent label fraction (78.9\%) is the primary diagnostic; DAF increases monotonically with $P$ (Appendix~\ref{app:penalty}). Preliminary pilots on MiniHack~\citep{minihack-2021} (0\% death) and Crafter~\citep{crafter-2022} (100\% death, both strategies) produced no death asymmetry, illustrating two boundary conditions: no death mechanism yields no signal (consistent with MATH); universal death lacks exploitable asymmetry. The framework requires an intermediate regime where strategy choice affects survival; NetHack~\citep{nethack-2020} combat tasks remain the most direct replication target \citep{balrog-2025,netplay-2024}.
